sections.h2: Who bills and who values property tax for a Dayton house?
sections.html:
Dayton is the seat of Montgomery County, so the Montgomery County Auditor values the house and the Montgomery County Treasurer sends the bill and collects it. Property tax in Dayton is a county matter. Taxpayer questions about a bill go to the treasurer's Taxpayer Services line at 937-225-4010, option 1, and questions about value go to the auditor at 937-225-4326.

The treasurer's office says it oversees collection on more than 250,000 real estate parcels across the county, which explains why most routine matters are handled by phone, online or by drop box rather than at a city counter.

sections.h2: When are Dayton property taxes due?
sections.html:
Montgomery County bills twice a year, with taxes due every February and July and bills arriving in January and June. For the 2026 collection, the first half was due February 13, 2026 and the second half July 24, 2026, and both dates have passed. Later years follow the same two-payment rhythm, and the treasurer posts a collection timeline each year.

The bill is also one full year behind. The treasurer explains that the first-half bill covers January through June of the year before, and the second-half bill covers July through December of that earlier year. Ask the treasurer which half-year periods a pending sale touches before you plan the closing.

  • There is no discount for paying the full year in February.
  • A 10 percent penalty applies to any first-half or second-half payment not paid in full by its due date.
  • The two halves can differ because some assessments appear on the first-half bill only.

sections.h2: What payment help does the Montgomery County Treasurer offer?
sections.html:
The treasurer runs a prepayment plan for owners with no past-due balance, with monthly billing that you can pay by mail or by withdrawal from an account. Enrollment must come at least 60 days before a due date, and current taxes must be paid first. Coupons go out at the start of March and the start of August.

For owners who are behind, the office offers delinquent payment plans. A plan brings you current by paying new taxes as they come due while paying off the older balance, with no additional interest and penalty accruing under the contract. If the county has sold a lien on your parcel, the treasurer cannot take payments on it. You deal with the lien holder, and the parcel record still shows "lien sold" until the lien is released, even after you pay the holder.

The treasurer's payment options page lists these channels:

  • Online and by phone.
  • Drop box, in person or by mail.
  • The monthly prepayment program and past-due payment plans.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Dayton property value?
sections.html:
Ask the Montgomery County Auditor's Board of Revision for a complaint application, which the treasurer's page says you can request by calling 937-496-6856. Under ORC 5715.19 the complaint is due by March 31 of the following tax year, or the close of first-half collection if that is later, and the treasurer's page describes the filing window as January 2 through March 31.

The board investigates and may hold a formal hearing, and the property owner carries the burden of justifying the complaint. The board may raise a value as well as lower it. Under the statute you may tender tax on your claimed value while the case is open, and the board must decide an original complaint within 180 days of the filing deadline.

A lower value does not guarantee a lower bill. The treasurer notes that taxes can rise even when value falls, because levies that pass in your school or local district raise the effective rate.

sections.h2: How do you change a mailing address or get payment records in Dayton?
sections.html:
Ohio law requires a change of mailing address for tax bills to be made in writing, and the Montgomery County Treasurer provides a Change of Address form for that purpose. Owners who are selling should send the form once a closing date is set so a late bill does not go to an empty house.

If a mortgage company pays your taxes through escrow, the amount withheld appears on the 1099 form the lender sends you. If you pay directly and lack records, call the treasurer at 937-225-4010, option 1, to request an itemization of payments, because the office does not mail one automatically. When a bill reaches you but a lender pays it, tell the lender you received a copy and they will ask the treasurer for their own.

The treasurer's page describes where the money goes: counties, cities, villages, school districts and special districts each raise money through real estate taxes, and the revenue pays for schools, police and fire protection, roads, libraries and parks.

sections.h2: Is there a senior or disability tax reduction in Dayton?
sections.html:
Yes. The Homestead Reduction Program is open to an owner who is 65 or older, or who is totally and permanently disabled, and only an owner-occupied primary residence qualifies. The treasurer's page points to the county homestead page for the application and current limits, so use that page or call the auditor before you assume you qualify.

The reduction matters at sale time because the seller and buyer must address it on the deed paperwork. Under ORC 319.202, the conveyance statement asks the seller whether the current or prior year's tax carries the reduction, and if it does, both sides sign a sworn statement that accounts for it. A buyer who is not eligible will see a higher bill than the seller did.

sections.h2: What is Dayton like for a seller, and how does that affect value?
sections.html:
Dayton was founded in 1796 on the Great Miami River and had 137,644 residents in the 2020 census, making it the sixth-largest city in Ohio. That census counted 57,751 households and 68,899 housing units, with 16.2 percent of units vacant and a median age of 34.9.

The city's ten historic neighborhoods include the Oregon District, Wright Dunbar, Dayton View, Grafton Hill, McPherson Town, Webster Station, Huffman, Kenilworth, St. Anne's Hill and South Park, and they hold many single-family houses in styles from Craftsman to Colonial Revival. Dayton Public Schools runs 34 schools, and the Dayton International Airport, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and the healthcare systems anchor local employment.

Two weather facts shape upkeep. The 1913 flood led to the Miami Conservancy District's dams and pumps, and the Memorial Day 2019 tornado outbreak produced an EF4 that crossed Dayton and nearby communities. Keep records of roof, drainage and basement repairs so a buyer can see what was done.

faqs.q: Does the City of Dayton collect property tax?
faqs.a: No. The Montgomery County Treasurer bills and collects the tax and the Montgomery County Auditor sets the value. Contact the treasurer's Taxpayer Services line at 937-225-4010, option 1, about a bill.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a Dayton property tax due date?
faqs.a: A 10 percent penalty applies to any first-half or second-half payment not paid in full by its due date. Call the treasurer's delinquency line at 937-225-4010, option 2, to ask about a payment plan.

faqs.q: Why is my Dayton tax bill a year behind?
faqs.a: Montgomery County bills one full year in arrears. The first-half bill covers January through June of the previous year and the second-half bill covers July through December of that year.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Dayton house if a tax lien was sold?
faqs.a: Yes, but the treasurer cannot take payments on a sold lien. Contact the lien holder for payoff terms and confirm the lien shows as released on the parcel record after payment.

faqs.q: How do I dispute my Dayton property value?
faqs.a: File a complaint with the Montgomery County Auditor's Board of Revision, which you can request by calling 937-496-6856. The filing deadline is March 31 of the following tax year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.
